subject: math
title: Grade 3 One-Step Equations
seo_title: Grade 3 One-Step Equations Worksheets: Free Math with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: One-step addition and subtraction equations with an unknown number
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on one-step equations for the BC curriculum: the equal sign as a balance, missing numbers like □ + 25 = 60 and 80 − □ = 35, writing equations for stories and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The equal sign means “is the same as”. To find the unknown, use the inverse: subtraction undoes addition.
key_sub: □ + 25 = 60, so □ = 60 − 25 = 35. □ − 15 = 40, so □ = 40 + 15 = 55. Put the number back in to check.
body_html:
The equal sign means “the same as”

An equation has an = sign. The = sign does not mean “the answer comes next”. It means both sides have the same value, like a pan balance that is level.

Find the unknown: use the inverse

A box □ stands for an unknown number. To find it, use the inverse, the operation that undoes it. Subtraction undoes addition, and addition undoes subtraction. Then put your answer back in to check.

EquationDo thisAnswer
□ + 25 = 6060 − 2535
80 − □ = 3580 − 3545
□ − 15 = 4040 + 1555
Example

80 − □ = 35

80 take away what leaves 35? Work out 80 − 35 = 45. Check: 80 − 45 = 35.

Answer: 45

Example

□ − 15 = 40

The box is the number you start with. Undo − 15 by adding: 40 + 15 = 55. Check: 55 − 15 = 40.

Answer: 55

Write an equation for a story

Use a box for the number you do not know. Joining or getting more is +. Taking away or getting off is −.

Example

45 bald eagles sit in the trees. Some fly away. Now 18 are left. How many flew away?

Equation: 45 − □ = 18. Work out 45 − 18 = 27. Check: 45 − 27 = 18.

Answer: 27 eagles

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
□ + 25 = 60, so □ = 85 (60 + 25)Use the inverse: 60 − 25 = 35
□ − 15 = 40, so □ = 25 (40 − 15)Undo − 15 by adding: 40 + 15 = 55
80 − □ = 35, so □ = 55 (smaller digit from larger)Regroup: 80 − 35 = 45
8 + 7 = 15 + 5 = 20= means “the same as”. Write two equations: 8 + 7 = 15, then 15 + 5 = 20

faq.q: What are one-step equations in Grade 3 math in BC?
faq.a: They are addition and subtraction equations with one unknown number, like □ + 25 = 60 or 80 − □ = 35. The BC Grade 3 Patterning standard asks students to solve them and write them for stories.

faq.q: How do you find the missing number in □ + 25 = 60?
faq.a: Use the inverse operation. Subtraction undoes addition, so □ = 60 − 25 = 35. Check by putting 35 back in: 35 + 25 = 60.

faq.q: What does the equal sign mean in Grade 3 math?
faq.a: The equal sign means “is the same as”, not “the answer is”. Both sides must have the same value, like a level pan balance: 8 + 6 = 10 + 4.

faq.q: How can I help my child turn a word problem into an equation?
faq.a: Ask what number is unknown and put a box there. Joining or getting more is +, taking away is −: “25 cards, gets some more, now 60” is 25 + □ = 60.

sets.title: Balances: the equal sign means “the same as”

items.q: The pans balance. Which equation matches?
items.e: The pans balance, so both sides have the same value. The left pan has 6 + 8 and the right pan has 14, so 6 + 8 = 14. The = sign can sit between any two things that are the same.

items.q: The pans balance. Which equation matches?

items.e: The pans balance. 30 − 10 = 20 and 15 + 5 = 20, so 30 − 10 = 15 + 5. The = sign means “is the same as”.

items.e: Work out both sides. 8 + 4 = 12 and 7 + 5 = 12, so 8 + 4 = 7 + 5 is true. 8 + 4 = 12 + 5 is false: 12 + 5 is 17.

Which has the same value as 6 + 9?

items.q: What does the = sign mean in 6 + 4 = 7 + 3?
items.e: = means “is the same as”. 6 + 4 = 10 and 7 + 3 = 10, so both sides are the same. It does not just mean “the answer comes next”.

items.q: Noah adds 8 and 7, then adds 5. He writes 8 + 7 = 15 + 5 = 20. What is wrong?
items.e: = means both sides are the same. 8 + 7 = 15, but 15 + 5 = 20, so “8 + 7 = 15 + 5” is not true. Noah should write two equations: 8 + 7 = 15 and 15 + 5 = 20.

sets.title: Write an equation for a story

items.q: Wei has 25 hockey cards. He gets some more. Now he has 60. Which equation matches?
items.e: Wei starts with 25, gets an unknown number more and ends with 60: 25 + □ = 60. 25 + 60 = □ is wrong: 60 is the total, not a part. Then □ = 60 − 25 = 35.

items.q: Ethan picks 36 blueberries. Then he picks 27 more. How many does he have in all? Which equation matches?
items.e: Joining 36 and 27 gives the total: 36 + 27 = □. So □ = 63.

items.q: There are 45 bald eagles in the trees near Squamish. Some fly away. Now 18 are left. Which equation matches?
items.e: Start with 45, take away an unknown number and 18 are left: 45 − □ = 18. Then □ = 45 − 18 = 27.

items.q: A SkyTrain car has 64 people on it. At the next station, 28 people get off. How many are on now? Which equation matches?
items.e: Start with 64 and take away 28: 64 − 28 = □. So □ = 36 people. Getting off means take away, not add.

items.q: Some children are playing at Stanley Park. 15 more children come. Now there are 42. Which equation matches?
items.e: The unknown is how many children were there at the start. Add 15 and you get 42: □ + 15 = 42. Then □ = 42 − 15 = 27.

items.q: There are 28 students in a class. 13 are on the red team. The rest are on the blue team. Which equation matches?
items.e: The red team and the blue team make the whole class: 13 + □ = 28. Then □ = 28 − 13 = 15.

items.q: Jasleen has some money. She spends $12 at the Richmond Night Market and has $25 left. Which equation matches?
items.e: The unknown is the money at the start. Take away $12 and $25 is left: □ − 12 = 25. Then □ = 25 + 12 = $37. 25 − 12 = □ uses the wrong operation.

items.q: Which equation means “a number plus 12 is 30”?
items.e: Use □ for the number. “Plus 12” is + 12 and “is 30” is = 30: □ + 12 = 30. Then □ = 18.

items.q: Which equation means “a number take away 8 is 25”?
items.e: Start with the number □, take away 8, and get 25: □ − 8 = 25. Then □ = 25 + 8 = 33. 8 − □ starts with 8, not with the number.

items.q: Which equation matches the bar model?
items.e: The two parts, 54 and □, make the whole, 90: 54 + □ = 90. Then □ = 90 − 54 = 36.

items.q: Which equation matches the bar model?
items.e: The box is the whole. The parts 36 and 48 join to make it: 36 + 48 = □. So □ = 84.

items.q: A BC Ferries boat has some cars on it. Then 140 more cars drive on. Now there are 400 cars. Which equation matches?
items.e: Some cars and 140 more make 400: □ + 140 = 400. Then □ = 400 − 140 = 260.

items.q: A Grade 3 class has raised $320 for the Terry Fox Run. The goal is $500. Which equation shows how much more they need?
items.e: What they have plus what they still need makes the goal: 320 + □ = 500. Then □ = 500 − 320 = $180.

items.q: The school library has 600 books. Some are checked out. 450 books are still on the shelves. Which equation matches?
items.e: Start with 600, take away the books checked out, and 450 are left: 600 − □ = 450. Then □ = 150.

items.q: Which equation matches the bar model?
items.e: The parts □ and 275 make the whole, 500: □ + 275 = 500. Then □ = 500 − 275 = 225.

items.q: Owen’s family drives 350 km from Vancouver to Kamloops. They stop in Hope after 150 km. Which equation shows how far they still have to drive?
items.e: They drove 150 km, they still have □ km, and the whole trip is 350 km: 150 + □ = 350. Then □ = 350 − 150 = 200 km.

items.q: Which story matches 60 − □ = 35?
c: 60 geese and 35 ducks are on a pond. How many birds are there?
Some geese are on a pond. 35 fly away. 60 are left. How many were there?
60 geese are on a pond. 35 more land. How many are there now?
60 geese are on a pond. Some fly away. 35 are left. How many flew away?
items.e: 60 − □ = 35 starts with 60, takes away an unknown number and leaves 35. That is the story where some geese fly away and 35 are left. Then □ = 60 − 35 = 25.

items.q: Which story matches □ + 18 = 50?
c: Simran has 18 stickers. She gets 50 more. How many does she have now?
Simran has 50 stickers. She gets 18 more. How many does she have now?
Simran has some stickers. She gives away 18. Now she has 50. How many did she have at first?
Simran has some stickers. She gets 18 more. Now she has 50. How many did she have at first?
items.e: □ + 18 = 50: an unknown start, plus 18, makes 50. That is the story where Simran has some stickers, gets 18 more and then has 50. Then □ = 50 − 18 = 32.

items.q: “48 people are on a SkyTrain. Some get off. Now 30 are on.” Leah writes 48 + 30 = □. Which equation should she write?
items.e: People get off, so it is take away. Start with 48, take away □, and 30 are left: 48 − □ = 30. Then □ = 18. 48 + 30 adds instead.

items.q: Olivia has 42 hockey cards. Ryan has 15 more cards than Olivia. Which equation shows how many cards Ryan has?
items.e: “15 more than 42” means add 15 to 42: 42 + 15 = □. So Ryan has 57 cards. 42 − 15 would give fewer cards, not more.

items.q: Mateo has 25 hockey cards. He gets some more. Now he has 60 cards. How many cards did he get?
items.e: Equation: 25 + □ = 60. Use the inverse: □ = 60 − 25 = 35 cards. Check: 25 + 35 = 60. Not 85: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 45: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.e: Equation: 26 + □ = 61. □ = 61 − 26 = 35 eagles. Check: 26 + 35 = 61. Not 87: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 45: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: A class counts 150 salmon in a creek on Monday. On Friday they count 320 salmon. How many more salmon do they count on Friday?
items.e: Equation: 150 + □ = 320. □ = 320 − 150 = 170 salmon. Check: 150 + 170 = 320. Not 470: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 230: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: A school has 400 students. 165 students walk to school. The rest come by bus or car. How many students come by bus or car?
items.e: Equation: 165 + □ = 400. □ = 400 − 165 = 235 students. Check: 165 + 235 = 400. Not 565: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 365: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: The school library has 500 books in the reading corner. 275 are in English and the rest are in French. How many books are in French?
items.e: Equation: 275 + □ = 500. □ = 500 − 275 = 225 books. Check: 275 + 225 = 500. Not 775: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 375: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: A hiking trail is 850 m long. A class has walked 475 m. How many metres do they still have to walk?
items.e: Equation: 475 + □ = 850. □ = 850 − 475 = 375 m. Check: 475 + 375 = 850. Not 1325 m: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 425 m: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: A ski hill has 600 pairs of rental skis. 385 pairs are rented out. How many pairs are left?
items.e: Equation: 600 − 385 = □. Work out 600 − 385 = 215 pairs. Check: 215 + 385 = 600. Not 985: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 385: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: A ferry to Vancouver Island has room for 400 cars. 265 cars are on it. How many more cars can drive on?
items.e: Equation: 265 + □ = 400. □ = 400 − 265 = 135 cars. Check: 265 + 135 = 400. Not 665: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 265: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of regrouping.

items.q: Kai gives away 45 stickers. Now he has 128 stickers. How many stickers did he have at the start?
items.e: Equation: □ − 45 = 128. Undo − 45 by adding: □ = 128 + 45 = 173 stickers. Check: 173 − 45 = 128. Not 83: that subtracts instead of adding. Not 163: that forgets to carry.

items.q: Arjun’s family drives from Vancouver to Kelowna, about 390 km. They stop in Merritt after 270 km. How many kilometres do they still have to drive?
items.e: Equation: 270 + □ = 390. □ = 390 − 270 = 120 km. Check: 270 + 120 = 390. Not 660 km: that adds instead of subtracting.

items.q: A school wants to collect 1000 cans for the food bank. So far it has 640 cans. How many more cans does it need?
items.e: Equation: 640 + □ = 1000. □ = 1000 − 640 = 360 cans. Check: 640 + 360 = 1000. Not 1640: that adds instead of subtracting. Not 460: count on from 640 to 700 (60), then from 700 to 1000 (300).
